conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you so much for making time today. I’m Dr. Ramirez, a perinatal-mental-health specialist. I work with new mothers to be sure they’re getting the emotional support they deserve after baby arrives.

To do that, I’d like to use a quick questionnaire called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s just ten questions about how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days; it helps us pick up on signs of depression, anxiety, and—importantly—any thoughts of self-harm so we can keep you safe. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me you might hurt yourself or someone else, in which case we’d make a safety plan together.

We’ll keep this conversational—no check-boxes on your end. I’ll ask each question in everyday language, and you can answer however feels most comfortable. Ready to start?

First question: Over the last week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt hard to do?

[soft half-smile, then sighs]

I’ve… I’ve laughed a couple of times, I guess—like when my sister sent that silly meme about new-mom life. But mostly it feels like I’m faking it. Things that used to crack me up just feel flat, or I’ll start to smile and then this wave of “what’s the point?” hits. So, yeah, it’s been pretty hard to find the funny side lately.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[slowly shakes head]

No… not really. I mean, maybe once or twice I’ve managed a little laugh, but it feels forced, like I’m just pretending. Most of the time nothing feels funny at all.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[shrugs, eyes on the floor]

Honestly… no. Even little things—like my favorite show coming on or a walk with the stroller—just feel like chores. I keep thinking, “I should be excited,” but the feeling never shows up.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[voice drops, fingers picking at sleeve]

Yeah… all the time. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t nap and I kept thinking it’s because I’m doing something wrong—maybe I’m not rocking him right or I ate something that upset him. My partner says I’m too hard on myself, but I can’t shake the guilt.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[exhales shakily]

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly my heart’s racing because what if he chokes? Or I’ll lie down and picture the bassinet collapsing, or him stopping breathing. Nothing specific happened—I just feel like danger’s around every corner.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah... a couple times this week. Once I was just folding laundry and my chest got tight, heart pounding—I had to set the basket down and breathe through my mouth like I was running a race. No warning, no real reason. It passed after a few minutes, but it left me shaky the rest of the afternoon.
Things have been getting on top of me

[quiet laugh, wipes eyes]

Most days, yeah. It feels like I’m drowning in bottles and diapers and laundry, and the minute I finish one thing two more pile up. I keep telling myself “just get through the next hour,” but the next hour feels impossible too.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[sighs, pulling cardigan tighter]

Yes… almost every night. I finally get him down, but then my head starts spinning—what if I’m a terrible mom, what if something happens to him, what if I never feel normal again? I lie there for hours, wide awake, even though I’m exhausted.
I have felt sad or miserable

[presses lips together, nods slowly]

Yeah… pretty much every day this week. It’s like a heavy blanket that won’t lift. I’ll be rocking the baby and tears just start rolling—no real trigger, just this constant ache.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes… I’ve cried a lot. Sometimes it’s because I’m overwhelmed, but other times the tears just come and I can’t stop them. I feel like I’m failing at everything, and the sadness feels so heavy I can’t hold it in.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]

No—never. I’ve felt low, but hurting myself has never crossed my mind. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom he deserves.

I hear how heavy the last week has felt for you-how laughter seems distant, even the smallest pleasures slip away, and waves of <sym>guilt</sym> and <sym>worry</sym> crash over you many times a day. You're working so hard to care for your baby while battling a constant <sym>low mood</sym>, <sym>panic-like episodes</sym>, and nights of restless <sym>insomnia</sym> filled with frightening thoughts. Your honesty about feeling overwhelmed yet determined to be the mom your son deserves shows remarkable strength, and you deserve support that lightens that load.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports almost no ability to laugh naturally and sees nothing funny, matching "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly says "no" and describes an almost complete absence of anticipatory enjoyment, matching "Hardly at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports blaming herself "all the time" and provides a specific example of persistent, self-critical thoughts, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, pervasive, intrusive worry without triggers, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete panic-like episodes (tight chest, pounding heart) occurring multiple times without provocation, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling overwhelmed "most days," uses metaphor of drowning, and describes inability to manage accumulating tasks, matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sleep difficulty "almost every night" due to racing anxious thoughts, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, persistent sadness with unexplained crying and a constant ache, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent uncontrollable crying and feeling overwhelmed, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS total of 26 far exceeds the ≥14 threshold indicating probable <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. All core-symptom items are scored maximum or near-maximum: <sym>loss of enjoyment</sym> (Q2=3), <sym>persistent sadness</sym> (Q8=3), <sym>excessive self-blame</sym> (Q3=3), and <sym>sleep disruption</sym> (Q7=3). Additional high scores on <sym>anxiety</sym> (Q4=3) and <sym>panic episodes</sym> (Q5=2) suggest co-occurring <med>postpartum anxiety</med>. No self-harm ideation (Q10=0) lowers acute safety risk yet severity warrants urgent intervention. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> for diagnostic evaluation and treatment planning
2. Ask about supports-partner, family, friends-and encourage accepting practical help with baby care, meals, and household tasks
3. Provide perinatal crisis line numbers (e.g., Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773) and local urgent mental-health contacts
4. Discuss evidence-based options: individual <med>CBT</med>, short-term <med>IPT</med>, or sertralantidepressant medication compatible with breastfeeding
5. Encourage 15-20 min daily outdoor walks and brief relaxation breathing to gently reduce <sym>arousal</sym>
6. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 1-2 weeks to monitor score trend and intervention response
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – Brief Summary

**Patient-reported symptoms:**  
- Marked anhedonia (minimal laughter, no anticipatory enjoyment)  
- Pervasive low mood, daily crying spells  
- Excessive, inappropriate guilt regarding infant care  
- Persistent, unprovoked anxiety (racing heart, catastrophic worries about infant safety)  
- Two recent panic-style episodes without clear trigger  
- Overwhelmed/drowning feeling most days  
- Sleep-onset insomnia tied to intrusive negative thoughts  
- No self-harm ideation (endorsed item 10 negative)  

**Pattern:** Consistent with significant postpartum depressive and anxious distress; daily functional impairment noted.  

**Risk flags:**  
– Depressed mood, loss of pleasure, guilt, concentration on perceived maternal “failures”  
– Anxiety/panic symptoms co-occurring with mood disturbance  
– Sleep disruption secondary to rumination  
– Absence of suicidal ideation at present time  

**Screening conclusion:** High level of distress; scores and clinical picture indicate need for prompt follow-up assessment for possible postpartum depression and/or anxiety disorder.
